tldr: This paper represents the core of manipulation—the movement trajectory of 3D contact points between a hand or gripper and an object—as Contact Flow, proposing a video world model trainable on both human and robot data. Because it does not depend on specific actuator shapes or joint spaces, it can be trained on a mix of human demonstrations and robot datasets, transferring zero-shot to unseen robots and environments for action verification.
hero_caption: The validation environment for the real-robot control loop using Contact Flow. A virtual twin environment is built from a single RGBD viewpoint, predicting contact points from the end-effector trajectory proposed by a policy model and simulating the future with a video world model.
overview:
Video-based world models, which allow robots to plan by predicting future outcomes before acting, have been attracting significant attention. However, existing video world models rely on representations tied to specific hardware—such as joint angles—or on visual features like end-effector silhouettes. As a result, they struggle to generalize across human and robot data, or even between different robot platforms.

To address this, the authors focused on a simple intuition: physical manipulation is governed by the contact points themselves, not by the appearance of the actor. The proposed representation, Contact Flow, is an extremely compact signal that projects onto the image plane only where an object's surface is touched and how those 3D contact points move alongside local displacements. By discarding the actor's own shape and kinematics, human hand manipulations and robot gripper grasps can be handled in the exact same format.

The authors automatically extracted Contact Flow from human-object interaction videos and robot teleoperation data, then trained a large-scale video generative model based on a Diffusion Transformer (DiT). They further built a pipeline that generates future rollouts from proposed trajectories and pre-verifies success or failure using a vision-language model (VLM). Experiments across the DROID dataset, multiple unseen benchmarks, and real-world tabletop manipulation tasks with a Franka Panda robot demonstrated that this approach enables accurate future prediction across embodiments as well as zero-shot action verification in unseen environments.
contributions: Proposal of Contact Flow, an embodiment-agnostic action representation based on 3D contact point trajectories and displacements that can be shared between humans and robots
Development of a generative architecture conditioning a large-scale video diffusion backbone on Contact Flow using two control injection mechanisms: ControlNet and VACE
Creation of a data processing pipeline that reliably and automatically extracts accurate Contact Flow from diverse human activity videos and robot manipulation datasets

Implementation and demonstration of a zero-shot action verification pipeline where a VLM pre-evaluates proposed trajectories on generated videos before executing them on a real robot in unseen environments

sections.heading: Stripping away the robot body to simulate contact itself
sections.summary: While video world models are valuable for robot planning and evaluation, they often struggle to capture physical contact correctly. This paper introduces Contact Flow, which discards actor appearance and joint kinematics to focus solely on the motion of contact points on object surfaces, unifying learning across human and robot data.
sections.details:
World models that simulate environmental dynamics in advance hold promise for a wide range of applications, including action planning, policy distillation, data augmentation, and safety verification. Although modern video generation models can produce realistic scenes, they frequently suffer from hallucinations that violate physical contact rules, making them unreliable as control models.

Conventional action-conditioning signals have two major shortcomings. One is joint-angle conditioning. While expressive, it strictly depends on a specific robot's joint structure and cannot transfer to different embodiments or human data. The other approach uses end-effector silhouettes or masks, but these remain overly tied to the actor's visual geometry rather than the critical interaction interface with the object.

This work centers on the fact that what dictates how an object moves is simply which physical contacts act upon it and how. Contact Flow formalizes this principle. By projecting 3D contact coordinates and their displacement vectors onto the image space, it creates a minimal signal that treats human hands and parallel-jaw grippers identically. Using this signal to condition a video generative model (Wan), the authors realized a safe pipeline that learns from mixed human and robot datasets, assesses generated rollout videos with a VLM, and only then executes them in the real world.

sections.heading: Evolution of video world models and cross-embodiment interfaces
sections.summary: The paper surveys prior work across video world models, controllable video generation, hand-object interaction analysis, and cross-embodiment adaptation. Unlike previous approaches that rely on actor shapes or whole-scene optical flow, this method stands out by isolating only the active contact interface for conditioning.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of four main research fields:

- Video world models for robotics: Efforts like UniPi, GR-1, and RoboDreamer use generated videos for action planning, policy learning, and data augmentation. However, most remain restricted to a specific robot's action space.
- Controllable video generation: Methods range from high-level semantic control using language instructions to spatial conditioning using end-effector states, full-body poses, depth maps, or optical flow. Yet, these signals are either too abstract or excessively tied to body morphology.
- Hand-object interaction (HOI) analysis: Studies such as ContactDB, ContactPose, and HACO detect or predict contact surfaces, but their goals are analysis and grasp synthesis, not repurposing contact as a control signal for video generation.
- Cross-embodiment adaptation: While approaches like Kinema4D condition on full 4D point clouds of the robot and BridgeV2W uses actor masks, both still depend on the morphology of the acting body. Other methods predict flow over the entire object, but Contact Flow differs fundamentally by isolating only the active, force-exerting contact interface as the conditioning signal.

sections.heading: Formulating Contact Flow and extracting it from human and robot data
sections.summary: Contact Flow is a 7-channel sparse signal consisting of an object's 3D contact position, its displacement to the next frame, and a confidence weight. Fed into a latent video diffusion model, it is trained via Flow Matching. In addition, geometry and foundation models are combined to reliably extract noise-resilient contact data from human videos and robot logs.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Contact Flow Encoding
Contact Flow captures where an agent contacts an object's interface and how that contact region moves over time. Crucially, it isolates active dynamics from passive dynamics (such as a door swinging open after a knob has been turned). At each time step $t$, it tracks 3D contact coordinates $(x, y, z)$ in the camera frame, displacements to the next frame $(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)$, and a confidence weight $w \in [0, 1]$. Projecting these onto the image plane via camera intrinsics $\mathbf{K}$ yields a 7-channel sparse control frame stacked across the sequence as $\mathbf{C}_{1:T}$. The confidence weight $w$ combines geometric proximity between the hand/gripper and the object with local displacement consistency and neighborhood density to suppress estimation noise.

### 3.2 CF World Model
The video generation backbone is a DiT-based latent video diffusion model. A pretrained VAE maps video frames to latent representations $\mathbf{z}_{0:T}$. Conditioned on the first-frame latent $z_0$ and the Contact Flow sequence $\mathbf{C}_{1:T}$, the model trains a target velocity field $v_\theta$ using a Flow Matching objective. To show that this approach is agnostic to specific control architectures, the authors evaluate both a ControlNet structure (duplicated encoder branch) and a VACE structure (lightweight Context Adapter).

### 3.3 Data Processing
A pipeline was built to extract consistent contact information across diverse data sources:
- Human demonstrations (3.3.1): Hand poses are estimated via HaMeR and fitted to MANO 3D meshes. Objects are segmented with SAM3, and contact regions are predicted using HACO. To avoid false positives from HACO, contacts are filtered out unless 3D hand-object distance is below a threshold and their 2D image projections overlap.
- Robot data (3.3.2): Assuming a static third-person camera and known URDF, objects are detected using WildDet3D. Contact points are extracted from real mask overlaps for the visible front finger and from geometric URDF rendering overlaps for the occluded rear finger.
- Inference (3.3.3): From a single stereo pair, FoundationStereo and SAM 3D-Objects reconstruct a 3D object model, registered via differentiable Gaussian Splatting (gsplat) into a millimeter-accurate digital twin. Ingesting an end-effector trajectory proposed by a policy model directly synthesizes the Contact Flow required for pre-verification.

sections.heading: Cross-embodiment prediction accuracy and zero-shot real-robot verification
sections.summary: The authors evaluated prediction performance on the DROID dataset and multiple unseen benchmarks, followed by real-robot validation on a Franka Panda. Contact Flow outperformed embodiment-dependent baselines in generation quality, and adding virtual verification with a VLM significantly improved real-world task success rates.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Training combined DROID, Taste-ROB, TACO, OakInk, and LIBERO. Comparisons included language-only TesserAct, robot action-embedding model CTRL-World, and the primary baseline Kinema4D, which conditions on full 4D robot point clouds. Evaluations used PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DreamSim (primary metric), FID, and FVD, masking out the robot and hands during evaluation to isolate pure environment and object dynamics.

### Results
- (Q1) Contact Conditioning Effectiveness and Generalization: On the DROID test set, the proposed method maintained coherent rollouts over long horizons (up to ~10 seconds at stride 3), significantly outperforming baselines like Kinema4D in DreamSim and PSNR. Furthermore, it generated stable rollouts across four unseen benchmarks and different robot morphologies without any additional fine-tuning.
- (Q2) Zero-shot Real-World Verification: In 10 unseen tabletop pick-and-place tasks with a real Franka Panda, candidate trajectories from the state-of-the-art VLA model $\pi_{0.5}$ were simulated using the Contact Flow world model, with Gemini (VLM) evaluating success or failure. The model correctly predicted execution outcomes in 8 of 10 trials (80% accuracy). While running $\pi_{0.5}$ directly within a coarse digital twin suffered from severe real-world gaps, pre-verifying actions through the video world model enabled safer and more dependable execution.

captions.F1: The tabletop task experimental setup using a real Franka Panda robot. Contact Flow is generated from proposed end-effector trajectories, the video world model simulates the predicted future (bottom), and real-world execution (top) proceeds only after a VLM verifies safety and success.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: real-time simulation and geometric dependencies
sections.summary: Contact Flow serves as an embodiment-agnostic, contact-centric action representation, enabling high-fidelity world modeling trained across human and robot datasets. Key remaining hurdles include diffusion inference latency and dependence on accurate camera calibration and 3D depth estimation.
sections.details:
By projecting 3D contact point trajectories—the physical foundation of manipulation—Contact Flow establishes a video world model freed from embodiment constraints. Learning from heterogeneous human and robot data, it supports dependable zero-shot action verification on unseen objects and environments.

However, several limitations remain before practical deployment. First, relying on a large-scale video diffusion model incurs heavy computational overhead, putting real-time online planning and replanning out of reach for now. Second, the accuracy of contact extraction depends heavily on upstream calibration, metric depth from FoundationStereo, and segmentation quality from SAM3. Finally, while the model reproduces visual interaction outcomes faithfully, contact-rich behaviors involving complex friction and deformation will require deeper physical grounding.

takeaways: Focusing conditioning signals on the movement of contact interfaces rather than joint angles or body silhouettes allows human and robot data to be treated under a single unified format.
Masking out actors (hands or grippers) during training and evaluation directs focus to object dynamics, substantially improving prediction quality.
Having a video world model and VLM jointly 'imagine and verify' trajectories proposed by a policy (like a VLA) before physical execution provides a practical safeguard for real-world deployment.
limitations: Inference computation for the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbone is too heavy to run inside real-time online control loops.
The system relies heavily on precise stereo camera calibration, metric depth estimation, and segmentation quality, making it vulnerable to failures in noisy environments.
While visual outcomes are predicted accurately, complex contact-rich physics such as fine frictional forces and micro-slipping are not strictly simulated.
